summary.headline: No Organization identity or Product/Offer markup anywhere -- every page carries the same generic WebPage/WebSite/navigation JSON-LD regardless of content — high severity, Add an Organization node (name, url, sameAs) to the site-wide template, and Product/Offer JSON-LD for each pricing plan, generated from the same plan data the page already renders.

findings.title: No Organization identity or Product/Offer markup anywhere -- every page carries the same generic WebPage/WebSite/navigation JSON-LD regardless of content
findings.evidence: All 15 sampled pages -- homepage, About, Pricing, Features, Support, and every /guides/* essay -- declare the identical JSON-LD type set: WebPage, WebSite, ItemList (a SiteNavigationElement menu). None contains an Organization node (no sameAs, despite the About page naming a real founder and a 27-year-old parent company, 37signals) and none contains Product or Offer markup. The Pricing page in particular states five distinct plans with concrete prices in visible text ($0, $25, $59, $99, $100/mo range depending on plan) and explicit claims ('No per-user fees', 'Simple fixed prices') but its own JSON-LD WebPage node carries none of this -- only a generic page description.

reproduction.observed: "@type":"ItemList", "@type":"SiteNavigationElement", "@type":"WebPage", "@type":"WebSite" -- the same four types found on every other sampled page
reproduction.expected: A Product node per plan with offers.price, offers.priceCurrency and offers.availability, plus an Organization node with sameAs

suggested_action.summary: Add an Organization node (name, url, sameAs) to the site-wide template, and Product/Offer JSON-LD for each pricing plan, generated from the same plan data the page already renders.
suggested_action.mechanism: The template emits one fixed JSON-LD shape (WebPage/WebSite/nav ItemList) regardless of page content, so no page -- including the one page whose entire purpose is stating prices -- ever gets type-specific markup. An assistant extracting facts via schema.org rather than parsing prose currently gets an identity-less, price-less description of every page on the site.
steps: Add a single Organization JSON-LD block (name, url, sameAs) to the shared template.
On the Pricing page specifically, emit one Product node per plan with an Offer (price, priceCurrency, availability) sourced from the same plan data already rendered in the visible plan cards.

findings.title: Homepage's visible text never plainly states what Basecamp is -- the only clear definitional sentence lives in an invisible meta tag
findings.evidence: The homepage's first 300+ words of visible body text open with rhetorical, conversational marketing copy ('Tell me if this sounds about right? Hey there... You're juggling people, projects, and expectations...') and never state, in a plain self-contained sentence, that Basecamp is a project-management/team-communication product -- the entity is described entirely through scenario and contrast, not definition. A genuinely clear definitional sentence does exist -- 'Basecamp puts everything you need to get work done in one place. It's the calm, organized way to manage projects, work with clients, and communicate company-wide.' -- but it appears only in the page's <meta name="description"> and og:description tags, not anywhere in the rendered, readable body a visitor (or a fetcher parsing visible text rather than meta tags) actually encounters. The <title> tag is bare ('Basecamp'), carrying no descriptive tagline either.

reproduction.observed: Visible body text opens with narrative/rhetorical copy, no plain 'Basecamp is a...' sentence
reproduction.expected: The same sentence already written in the meta description, present as ordinary visible text near the top of the page

suggested_action.summary: Move (or duplicate) the existing meta-description sentence into the visible page as ordinary text near the top of the homepage.
suggested_action.mechanism: The well-written definitional sentence already exists and does not need to be composed from scratch -- it needs to also exist somewhere a reader (human or machine) parsing the rendered page's own text will actually encounter it, rather than only in a tag most readers never see.
steps: Add the existing meta-description sentence (or a close variant) as a visible line near the top of the homepage, before or alongside the current narrative opening.
Keep the narrative copy that follows -- it is not the defect; the absence of a plain sentence anywhere in the visible text is.
suggested_action.verification: curl -s https://basecamp.com | grep -o 'manage projects' returns a match inside the visible body, not only inside a <meta> tag.

findings.title: Pricing page's own JSON-LD description is broken -- a failed template interpolation dropped both price numbers, leaving a nonsensical fragment
findings.evidence: The WebPage node's description field on https://basecamp.com/pricing reads exactly: "Start free with Basecamp \u2014 one project, five users, forever free. Paid plans run  to /mo, all fixed price with no per-user fees." -- note the double space and the bare "/mo" where a price range should be (e.g. "$25 to $299/mo"). The visible page itself states real, correct prices ($25, $59, $99, $100, $299, $300 across the five plans), so this is not a missing-data problem -- the source values exist and render correctly elsewhere on the same page -- but a broken interpolation specific to this one description string. The About page's equivalent description field, by contrast, is well-formed prose with no missing values, confirming the defect is isolated to the pricing template's price-range substitution rather than the description field mechanism generally.

reproduction.observed: "description":"Start free with Basecamp \u2014 one project, five users, forever free. Paid plans run  to /mo, all fixed price with no per-user fees."
reproduction.expected: A complete sentence with both price bounds present, e.g. '...Paid plans run $25 to $299/mo...'

suggested_action.summary: Fix the price-range template variables feeding the Pricing page's JSON-LD description so both bounds populate, and add an automated check that fails the build if any JSON-LD field renders with adjacent whitespace where a value was expected.
suggested_action.mechanism: A broken machine-readable field is worse than an absent one: an assistant that trusts the markup over the prose gets a nonsensical price claim rather than no claim at all, on the one page whose entire purpose is stating price. Since the correct values already render in visible text on the same request, the fix is wiring the description template to the same values, not sourcing new data.
steps: Locate the price-range interpolation feeding the Pricing page's meta/JSON-LD description template.
Point it at the same price values already rendered in the visible plan cards.
Add a lint check (or a simple regex assertion in CI) that flags any emitted JSON-LD field containing two consecutive spaces or a currency symbol/unit with no adjacent digits.
suggested_action.verification: curl -s https://basecamp.com/pricing | grep -o '"description":"[^"]*"' contains both a leading and trailing price figure with no double space.

findings.title: Pricing page's weekly signup counter carries no recency signal, and its current value warrants verification
findings.evidence: The Pricing page states '2,026 organizations signed up last week.' -- the class name marks this explicitly as a dynamic, live-updating value, and the surrounding copy ('last week') asserts it changes on a rolling basis, yet nothing on the page states when it was last refreshed. Separately, and offered here as an observation rather than a claim: the displayed figure, 2,026, is digit-for-digit identical to the current year (2026), on the same page already confirmed to have a broken template-interpolation defect in its JSON-LD description (see the structured-data-audit finding). The two together are circumstantial, not proof, but worth the site owner's own verification that this counter is populating from live signup data rather than a stale fallback.

reproduction.expected: The same element, ideally with an adjacent 'as of <date>' signal, and a value confirmed to be live rather than a static fallback

suggested_action.summary: Verify the signup-count data pipeline is actually live (re-check the value on a later date and confirm it moves), and add a visible or machine-readable 'as of' timestamp next to the figure.
suggested_action.mechanism: A claim that is supposed to update weekly but carries no timestamp gives a reader -- human or assistant -- no way to tell whether it is current without a fresh fetch; pairing it with a dateModified or a visible 'as of' label closes that gap regardless of whether the current value turns out to be correct.
steps: Confirm server-side that the signup counter is reading from a live data source, not a cached or default value.
Add a machine-readable timestamp (a dateModified on the containing element, or a JSON-LD property) alongside the figure.
suggested_action.verification: Re-fetch the page on a later date; the displayed figure differs from 2,026 and a recency signal is present.

opportunities.title: Publish an llms.txt pointing at the /guides essays, Pricing, and Features
opportunities.rationale: The /guides/* essays (on shipping principles, decision-making, why group chat causes problems) are genuinely substantive, well-written reasoning pieces -- exactly the kind of primary-source content an assistant answering a 'why is X better than Slack' or 'how should teams communicate' question would want to cite directly, distinct from a generic marketing page.
opportunities.mechanism: llms.txt gives a retrieval-capable assistant a curated entry point to the site's actual reasoning and pricing facts, rather than requiring it to guess which of many marketing pages is worth citing.
steps: List Pricing, Features, and each /guides/* essay as top entries.
Keep descriptions one line each, naming the specific question each essay actually answers.

opportunities.title: Add explicit head-to-head comparison framing to the existing group-chat-problems essay
opportunities.rationale: The /guides/group-chat-problems essay already contains the reasoning for why Basecamp's model beats a pure group-chat tool, but it is not framed as an explicit comparison -- there is no heading shaped like 'Basecamp vs Slack' or a direct side-by-side. Users very commonly ask assistants comparison questions by name ('Is Basecamp better than Slack for project management?'), and an essay containing the right reasoning but not the expected question shape is a missed opportunity, not a defect.
opportunities.mechanism: A question-shaped heading naming the actual tools being compared gives an assistant a direct passage to lift for a comparison query, rather than requiring it to infer the comparison from an essay that never names the alternative explicitly.
steps: Add one or two comparison-shaped subheadings (e.g. naming the class of tool being contrasted) to the existing essay.
No new reasoning is needed -- the essay's existing content already supports this framing.

not_assessed.reason: Not performed in this run to stay within the demonstration's time budget -- no external domains were queried.
not_assessed.impact: Cannot confirm or rule out whether Basecamp/37signals's core claims are corroborated or contradicted on independent sources.

not_assessed.reason: Judged informally rather than through the full procedure: 'Basecamp' the common English word (a mountaineering/expedition term) does present a real collision risk in principle, but the product's long-established public dominance was judged sufficient to avoid practical ambiguity within this run's budget. The site provides no sameAs or Wikidata anchor either way, so this judgment is not independently verified.
not_assessed.impact: A formal check would give a verified answer rather than an informal one; the absence of any identity anchor (already noted in the structured-data finding) is the more actionable fact regardless of how this check resolves.

not_assessed.check: Question-coverage probe (answerability-audit, check 1) -- full 8-12 question set
not_assessed.reason: Roughly 8 plausible questions were checked directly against sampled pages (what is Basecamp, cost, free plan, per-user fees, comparison to chat tools, founders, keyboard shortcuts); questions about specific integrations, mobile apps, or data export were not checked.
not_assessed.impact: Coverage percentage should be treated as a lower bound from the questions actually verified, not a formal complete count.
